items.quote: Then he called two of his centurions and ordered them, “Get ready a detachment of two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea at nine tonight.
items.contrast: The centurions receive the order; the soldiers are members of the detachment they must prepare.
items.reason: “Them” refers to the two centurions just called, making them the recipients of the order. The question clearly tests recipient versus contents of the ordered detachment.

items.quote: We have seen the land, and it is very good. Aren’t you going to do something? Don’t hesitate to go there and take it over.
items.contrast: “It” refers to the land, not to the unsuspecting people found there.
items.reason: The singular land is introduced immediately before the instruction to take “it” over. Resolving that reference distinguishes the territory from its inhabitants.

items.quote: Jehoiada then made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.
items.contrast: The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people; the second includes only the king and people.
items.reason: The two successive covenants have different parties, so identifying the first requires keeping their order and participants distinct.

items.quote: When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him. As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was left lying on the road, with both the donkey and the lion standing beside it.
items.contrast: The departing man of God is killed; the prophet who saddled the donkey for him is not the victim.
items.reason: The prophet prepares the donkey for the man of God, after which the beneficiary goes on his way and is killed. The question tests resolution of the male pronouns between the two men.

items.quote: Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
items.contrast: Uzziah is eager to leave because of the Lord’s affliction, not merely because the priests are hurrying him out.
items.reason: The passage explicitly attaches Uzziah’s eagerness to the Lord’s affliction with “because.” This distinguishes the stated cause from the priests’ simultaneous response.
